body:
You found a place you can afford. The listing says $1,400 a month, and your budget says that works. Then the landlord hands you the move-in breakdown, and the number is more than double the rent. That gap surprises almost every first-time renter.

First apartment costs are everything you pay before you get the keys, plus the first round of bills that land in the same month. This guide adds them all up for you, with a full cost table, a worked example with real numbers, and a first-month checklist, so you know the real number before you sign anything.

## What first apartment costs actually include

First apartment costs are the one-time and first-month payments you make to move into a rental. They include first month's rent, a security deposit, application and admin fees, utility deposits and setup charges, renters insurance, moving costs, and basic furniture and household essentials. Some landlords also ask for last month's rent upfront. Added together, these usually come to two to four times the monthly rent, which is why the listing price alone never tells the full story.

## The full list of first apartment costs

Here is every charge that can show up, with typical ranges. Not every apartment has every fee, so use this table as a checklist and cross off the ones that do not apply to your place.

| Cost                   | What it is                                    | Typical range                                          | Refundable?            |
|----------------------------|---------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------|
| First month's rent         | Rent for your first month                         | One month's rent                                           | No                         |
| Security deposit           | Held against damage or unpaid rent                | $750 median (Zillow 2024), often one month's rent         | Usually yes                |
| Last month's rent          | Covers your final month, if required              | One month's rent                                           | No, it pays a future month |
| Application fee            | Credit and background check                       | Around $50                                                | No                         |
| Admin or move-in fee       | Lease processing, unit prep, keys                 | $100 to $300                                             | No                         |
| Broker fee                 | In a few cities, mostly New York City             | Up to one month's rent                                     | No                         |
| Utility deposits and setup | Electricity, gas, water, internet                 | $0 to $300                                               | Sometimes                  |
| Renters insurance          | Covers your belongings and liability              | About $171 per year                                       | No                         |
| Moving costs               | Truck, boxes, supplies, or movers                 | About $500 for a local DIY move                           | No                         |
| Furniture and essentials   | Bed, curtains, cleaning supplies, first groceries | $300 to $1,000+                                          | No                         |
| Pet deposit and pet rent   | If you have a pet                                 | $250 to $500 deposit, plus $25 to $65 monthly pet rent | Deposit sometimes          |

### Rent and deposit

First month's rent is due when you sign or when you get the keys. The security deposit is money the landlord holds against damage or unpaid rent, and you usually get it back when you move out if the place is in good shape. Zillow's Housing Trends Report 2024 puts the median security deposit for an apartment at $750, but many landlords charge a full month's rent instead. Deposit caps vary by state. In California and New York, the cap is one month's rent in most cases, while other states, including Florida and Texas, set no limit at all. Check your state's rule before you agree to a deposit that looks high.

Some landlords also ask for last month's rent upfront. That payment is not a second deposit. It covers your final month, so you do not pay rent again when you move out. If your lease asks for first month, last month, and a deposit, you are paying three months of rent before you unpack a single box.

### Fees and paperwork

The application fee covers the credit check and background check, and Zillow puts the typical fee at around $50. Admin or move-in fees are separate charges for processing the lease, preparing the unit, and handing over keys. They often run $100 to $300 and, unlike the deposit, you do not get them back. In a few cities, mostly New York City, a broker fee can add up to one month's rent. If your listing mentions a broker fee, ask who pays it before you apply.

### Utilities, insurance, and moving

Utilities often need deposits or setup fees, especially if you have no account history with the provider. Budget $0 to $300 for electricity, gas, water, and internet setup combined. Renters insurance is another small but real cost. NAIC data cited by the Insurance Information Institute puts the national average premium at about $171 a year, or roughly $14 a month, and many leases require it. Moving costs depend on how far you go and who carries the boxes. Zillow estimates about $500 for a local do-it-yourself move within 5 to 10 miles, while hiring movers costs more. Add boxes, tape, and cleaning supplies, and a cheap move still costs something.

### Furniture and the first grocery run

An empty apartment needs more than furniture. You need a shower curtain, a trash can, cleaning supplies, toilet paper, light bulbs, and food for the first week. If you buy a bed, a table, and a few basics secondhand, $300 to $500 can cover the essentials. Buying everything new at once can easily pass $1,000, so spread it out. Sleep on a mattress on the floor for a week if you have to. Nobody ever went broke from a late coffee table.

### Pets

If you have a pet, expect a pet deposit of $250 to $500, plus monthly pet rent of $25 to $65 in many buildings. Some landlords charge a non-refundable pet fee instead of a deposit. Ask which one applies, because a fee never comes back and a deposit might.

## A worked example: moving into a $1,400 apartment

This is an illustration with made-up numbers. It shows how the costs stack up for one renter moving into a $1,400-a-month apartment with no pets and no broker fee.

| Move-in cost                    | Amount |
|-------------------------------------|------------|
| First month's rent                  | $1,400    |
| Security deposit (one month's rent) | $1,400    |
| Application fee                     | $50       |
| Admin / move-in fee                 | $150      |
| Utility deposits and setup          | $200      |
| Renters insurance (first year)      | $171      |
| Moving (DIY truck, boxes, supplies) | $300      |
| Furniture and household essentials  | $400      |
| Total                               | $4,071    |

Check the math: $1,400 plus $1,400 is $2,800. Add $50, $150, $200, $171, $300, and $400, and you land on $4,071. That is nearly three times the monthly rent, and it does not include last month's rent. If the landlord also asks for last month upfront, add another $1,400, and the total becomes $5,471.

Your number will be different. A roommate cuts the rent, deposit, and moving costs in half. [How to split bills with roommates](/blog/how-to-split-bills-with-roommates/) shows how to divide those shared costs fairly. A higher rent or a broker fee pushes the total up fast. Run your own numbers with the table above before you sign.

## How much should you save before you move out?

A simple target is your upfront costs, plus one month of living expenses, plus a small cushion for surprises. For the example above, that means about $4,071 upfront, plus roughly $2,000 for the first month of food, transport, phone, and bills, plus a cushion of $500 to $1,000. That puts the savings target near $6,500 to $7,000.

If that number feels out of reach, you are not alone. Save for the move the same way you would save for any big planned cost: a fixed amount each month into a separate pot. [Sinking funds for beginners](/blog/sinking-funds-for-beginners/) walks through that method. And once you are in, start rebuilding a safety net. [How to build an emergency fund on a small income](/blog/emergency-fund-on-a-small-income/) shows how to do it on a tight budget.

## First-month budget checklist

Moving in is only half the bill. These monthly costs start in month one, so they belong in the same plan.

- Rent: $1,400 in this example
- Utilities: around $150 a month on average, per Zillow, for electricity, gas, water, and trash
- Renters insurance: about $14 a month
- Internet: $50 to $80, depending on the plan and the city
- Groceries: $200 to $300 for one person cooking most meals
- Transport: bus pass, gas, or rideshares
- Phone: your current plan
- Household basics: cleaning supplies, toilet paper, laundry

Add them up before you sign, not after. If the monthly total leaves nothing for food and transport, the apartment is too expensive, no matter how good the upfront deal looks. [How to budget on less than $1,000 a month](/blog/budget-on-less-than-1000-a-month/) shows how to build a monthly plan around a small income.

## Ways to lower your upfront bill

- Get a roommate. You split the rent, the deposit, the moving truck, and the internet bill.
- Ask what is included. If water, trash, or parking is in the rent, that is money you do not spend twice.
- Move yourself with friends. A rented truck and pizza for your helpers beats a full-service mover.
- Buy furniture secondhand. Thrift stores, marketplace listings, and friends getting rid of stuff cover most of it.
- Time it right. Moving at the end of the month or mid-week is often cheaper for trucks and movers.
- Read the fee list before you apply. Application fees are usually non-refundable, so do not pay them for five apartments at once.

## Mistakes that catch first-time renters

**Forgetting utility deposits.** A $200 deposit from the electric company on move-in week hurts when the budget is already empty. Call the providers before moving day and ask what they need upfront.

**Assuming the deposit comes back fast.** Your deposit does not come back the day you move out. Landlords get a window to inspect the unit and send an itemized list of deductions, and that window varies by state. Take dated photos at move-in and move-out so you can challenge any deduction that is not fair.

**Signing without reading the fee list.** Admin fees, pet fees, parking fees, and amenity fees can add hundreds to the total. Ask for every fee in writing before you hand over any money.

**Furnishing everything on day one.** You need a bed, a shower curtain, and a way to cook. The rest can wait a paycheck or two. A half-empty apartment for a month beats a maxed-out credit card.

**Moving in with zero cushion.** Something always costs more than planned: a longer truck rental, a forgotten deposit, a broken kettle. A few hundred dollars of cushion turns those into annoyances instead of emergencies.

## Frequently asked questions

### How much money do you need to move into your first apartment?

Plan on two to four times the monthly rent upfront. For a $1,400 apartment, that is roughly $2,800 to $5,600, depending on the deposit, whether last month's rent is required, and what the move costs. Add one month of living expenses and a small cushion on top of that.

### Is the security deposit refundable?

Usually yes, if you pay your rent on time and leave the place in good shape. The landlord can deduct for damage beyond normal wear and tear or for unpaid rent, and must send you an itemized list of any deductions. Rules and deadlines vary by state.

### Do I need first and last month's rent?

It depends on the landlord and your state. Many landlords ask for first month plus a deposit only. Some ask for last month too, which adds a full month of rent to your upfront total. In some states, last month's rent counts toward the deposit cap, so the landlord cannot charge both at the maximum. Ask what each payment covers before you sign.

### Can I move in with no savings?

It is risky. Without savings, one surprise fee or a late paycheck can leave you short on rent in the first month. If you must move now, get a roommate, keep the move as cheap as possible, and build a small cushion as fast as you can after you move in.

### How much is renters insurance for a first apartment?

About $171 a year on average in the US, or roughly $14 a month, based on NAIC data cited by the Insurance Information Institute. Your price depends on your city, your coverage limits, and your deductible. Many leases require it, so budget for it from month one.

## Your next step

Pick an apartment price, run your own numbers through the table above, and save toward that total before you start touring. Knowing your real first apartment costs turns apartment hunting from a guessing game into a plan.
